newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine not sure it can shut Chernobyl reactor.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine not sure it can shut Chernobyl reactor.

text.p: Ukraine, which promised the West it would close one reactor at the stricken Chernobyl nuclear plant this month, now believes it could be too dangerous to go through with its pledge, a Ukrainian official said on Tuesday.

"If this block stops and Chernobyl ends up in a situation where there is no heat to warm the station, then that could endanger the block and make the station prone to an accident," Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko told reporters.
Kostenko was speaking after a Paris meeting between Ukraine and nuclear experts from the Group of Seven leading industrial nations to discuss the plant's closure.

Ukraine, which has promised to close the station by 2000 in exchange for some $3 billion in grants and funding from the G7, gave assurances to G7 leaders in April that it would close the reactor this month.
But Kostenko, Ukraine's top negotiator on Chernobyl, said that the latest G7 meeting had not finalised a closure plan for the reactor. "We did not come to an agreement on stopping the first block."

He said that in the circumstances, the Ukrainian authorities had several options. "We can choose not to stop the first block. We can instead of the first block let the second block run. There are various ways to see this situation," he said.
Analysts say starting the second reactor, closed in 1991 after a fire, would require a lot of money, which Chernobyl does not have.

"At this moment the decision is made and the station is preparing to close the first block by the end of October," Kostenko said. "But on the other hand only one block running at Chernobyl is dangerous."
Two working RBMK-type reactors at Chernobyl, No. 1 and No. 3, produce five percent of Ukraine's electricity. The fourth block blew up 10 years ago in the world's worst civil nuclear accident.
Ukraine has repeatedly complained about the West's failure to deliver money for the closure of the plant, but Kostenko said the latest G7 meeting had been productive.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) would soon grant money to construct two reactors at the Kmelnytsky and Rivne stations in western Ukraine, to replace electricity lost by Chernobyl's closure.
"We will receive $600 to 800 million from the EBRD to finish the blocks," said Kostenko. "Talks will be solved by the end of this year and we will see financing next year.
"We can say that we did not get straight political talk this time, but that real steps are being taken for real economic support."
The EBRD also agreed to deliver 118.5 million Ecus ($150 million) by January 1, 1997 towards closure.

Both sides also discussed construction of a new "sarcophagus" over the ruined fourth reactor, including covering it with a hermetic seal. Storage of an estimated 90 to 200 tonnes of nuclear fuel inside the cracked sarcophagus was still under discussion, he said.

Kostenko added that all sides agreed to fund the creation of a special nuclear research centre, and said Ukraine was currently seeking $20 million to complete a hotel and office complex in the nearby town of Slavutych to serve visiting scientists.
Slavutych was hurriedly erected after the accident to house workers at the Chernobyl plant. Kostenko said that the G7 experts would meet again in Slavutych in December.
